prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Document units:
U0074: Individual flights can be omitted from the group by checking the “remove” box on this list.
U0075: The upper portion of the Graphical User Interface (GUI) includes a trial planner interface in the left pane, with active flight plan and trial-plan (recommended reroute) sector loading maps in the right panes.
U0076: As the trial plan modifications are made, all information related to the reroute is updated accordingly, providing the user with immediate feedback and enhanced situational awareness.
U0077: Yellow-colored sectors indicate that demand is predicted to exceed sector capacity, but some of the flights are not yet airborne.
U0078: Red-colored sectors indicate that demand is predicted to exceed sector capacity and all of the flights are currently airborne, which implies a higher level of confidence in the prediction.
U0079: Various factors impact sector capacity, but not all of those are known to automation systems.
U0080: Rather than routing around congested sectors, MFCR presents sector congestion information in the GUI, allowing the user to evaluate and modify the routing based on operational need.
U0081: Figure 3: MFCR Display Once the traffic managers find a recommendation to be operationally suitable, they coordinate with Area Supervisors for the sectors that currently control the flights in the group, as well as with traffic managers in other facilities that would be affected by the recommended reroute.
U0082: Coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) may also be necessary.
U0083: This coordination could take place via customary voice communication or by integrating automation, such as the Advanced Flight-Specific Trajectories (AFST, formerly Strategic Traffic Flow Management Application (SFMA)), and/or the MFCR interface itself [6].
U0084: When the traffic manager accepts the MFCR recommendation via the GUI, the corresponding flight plan amendments are sent to the air traffic displays of the appropriate sector controllers by using the AirBorne ReRoute (ABRR) capability.
U0085: The sector controllers then offer the reroute to the pilots of the affected flights via Data Comm or voice communications.
U0086: The flight crews coordinate their proposed reroutes with their dispatchers, if necessary, and once the flight crews accept the new routes, the sector controller(s) implement the corresponding flight plan amendment in the automation system.
U0087: In Figure 3, the green routes depict the current flight plan routes.
U0088: In this example, these routes represent “LEV West Partial” playbook routes, which are typically used when a large weather system in the south-central U.S. blocks transcontinental traffic.
U0089: These playbook routes merge westbound traffic from the southeastern U.S. at Three Rivers, TX (THX) and send the traffic via intermediate waypoints to El Paso, TX (ELP), after which traffic follows standard jet routes to destinations in the western U.S.
U0090: In the illustration, these routes are still in effect even though the weather has moved to the north, as depicted by yellow, orange, and red contours in the large map on the left of the figure.
U0091: This capability presents an opportunity for time-saving, constraint-free MFCR reroute recommendations, shown by yellow lines.
U0092: The MFCR recommendation in Figure 3 identifies nine flights in Houston Center that are recommended to be merged at fix LEJON, the Merge Point, and then sent direct to ELP, the Return Capture Fix.
U0093: The new routes of these nine flights are estimated to provide a total time savings of 53 minutes at an average of about 6 min per flight.
U0094: These flights have been organized into a new flow along the common route segment from LEJON to ELP.
U0095: If this new flow continues to be free of weather, there is also an opportunity to update the playbook routes assigned to other flights and provide time savings to aircraft that are currently upstream of this route modification.
U0096: This option would provide a beneficial intermediate routing solution prior to lifting the playbook restriction entirely when the weather dissipates fully.
U0097: Traffic managers may also access the MFCR savings decay feature that shows approximately how the overall savings of a recommended reroute group would decline as the implementation of a recommended reroute is delayed; Figure 4 shows an example.
U0098: One reason for delaying the issuance of a reroute would be the need to perform other, more urgent traffic management tasks.
U0099: The savings decay graph provides TMCs with a decision aid to determine how long they have to respond to the reroute recommendation before significant potential savings are lost.
U0100: Another reason to delay responding to a recommended reroute would be to wait for additional flights that will soon enter the Center to join the reroute group.
